title: Why are carboxylic acids acidic? The carboxyl group, its naming, its dimers and the proton it gives away
subtitle: Ethanoic acid and propan-1-ol have the same molar mass, and both contain an O–H group. Yet the acid boils 21 degrees higher, turns blue litmus red and fizzes with baking soda, while the alcohol does none of these. What does the carboxyl group change, and why does it make the molecule an acid?
subject: Chemistry
lessonIntent: identifying and drawing the carboxyl group; naming carboxylic acids up to C8 with methyl or ethyl branches; explaining their boiling points and solubility against other families and within the series; explaining why a carboxylic acid is a weak acid and an alcohol is not, using the conjugate base's shared charge and pKa; describing the litmus and hydrogen carbonate observations and writing the reactions with sodium hydroxide, magnesium and sodium hydrogen carbonate. No organic bases, no esters.

voiceover.text: In the alcohol reactions video, ethanol was oxidised under reflux, all the way to ethanoic acid. That's the acid in vinegar. Now compare it with propan-one-ol. Both have a molar mass of sixty, and both contain an O H group. Yet the acid boils at one hundred and eighteen degrees, and the alcohol at ninety seven. The acid turns blue litmus red, and it fizzes with baking soda. The alcohol does neither. So what does the acid's group change?

The acid's group is the carboxyl group, C O O H. It's a carbonyl, C double bond O, and an O H, both on the same carbon. So the two oxygens aren't alike. One is double bonded to carbon, and only the other carries a hydrogen. There's just one O H. Inside the molecule, these are covalent bonds, and both the C double bond O and the O H are polar.

To name one, find the longest chain that includes the carboxyl carbon. Drop the alkane's final e, and add oic acid. The carboxyl carbon is always carbon one, so there's no number: methanoic, ethanoic, propanoic, butanoic acid. Count that carbon in the chain. Ethanoic acid has two carbons. Branches are numbered from the carboxyl end, so this is two-methylpropanoic acid.

Now the boiling points. An alcohol's O H can give and take hydrogen bonds, and so can the acid's, so that alone isn't the difference. The difference is the C double bond O right beside the O H. The O H gives a hydrogen bond, and the oxygen of the C double bond O takes one. So two acid molecules can face each other and lock together with two hydrogen bonds. That pair is called a dimer. Add dipole-dipole forces from the C double bond O, and acid molecules attract each other more strongly. More energy is needed to pull them apart, so the acid boils higher.

Within the family, the pattern is like the alcohols. Each extra C H two adds dispersion forces, so boiling points climb. Methanoic acid boils at about one hundred degrees, ethanoic at one hundred and eighteen, propanoic at one hundred and forty one, and butanoic at about one hundred and sixty four. The carboxyl group hydrogen bonds with water, so the small acids, up to butanoic, mix with water. After that, the long non-polar chain wins, and solubility falls.

So why is it an acid? In water, the O H hydrogen can leave as a proton, H plus, and join a water molecule. That makes hydronium, and an ethanoate ion, C H three C O O minus. But the reaction is reversible, and the equilibrium lies well to the left. Ethanoate ions keep taking protons back, so most molecules stay whole. From the strength video, at point one moles per litre, ethanoic acid's pH is about two point nine. Only about one molecule in eighty has given its proton away. So ethanoic acid is a weak acid. Weak means partly ionised, not dilute.

But why does the acid's O H let go, when an alcohol's barely does? Look at what's left behind, the conjugate base. When ethanoic acid loses its proton, the C double bond O right beside that oxygen lets the negative charge spread across both oxygens, about half on each. Half a charge pulls on a proton less strongly, so ethanoate takes protons back less readily. An alcohol has no C double bond O there, so the whole charge would sit on one oxygen, and it would snatch the proton straight back. That's why ethanoic acid's p K a is about four point seven, and an alcohol's is about sixteen.

You can see the difference. A drop of ethanoic acid solution turns blue litmus red, because the acid has raised the hydronium ion concentration. A drop of propan-one-ol leaves it blue. On its own, the alcohol is about as neutral as water.

It also reacts like the acids from Module six. With sodium hydroxide, it's neutralised, forming water and a salt, sodium ethanoate. The salt's name swaps oic acid for oate. With magnesium, it reacts more slowly than a strong acid at the same concentration, forming magnesium ethanoate, and hydrogen gas bubbles off.

The most useful test is sodium hydrogen carbonate, baking soda. Ethanoic acid is a stronger acid than carbonic acid, so it passes a proton to hydrogen carbonate. The carbonic acid that forms breaks up into water and carbon dioxide, so it fizzes. An alcohol is far too weak, so nothing happens. In this course, if an organic compound fizzes with sodium hydrogen carbonate, it's a carboxylic acid. Just don't forget the C O two in the equation.

So, a carboxyl group is a C double bond O and an O H on one carbon, and the names end in oic acid. For molecules of similar size, carboxylic acid beats alcohol, beats aldehyde or ketone, beats alkane, because acid pairs hydrogen bond twice. And it's acidic because the charge left behind is shared, which loosens its grip on the proton. Share the charge, loosen the grip.

Your turn. Compound X has the condensed formula shown, and it boils at one hundred and seventy seven degrees. Hexan-one-ol, with a similar molar mass, boils at one hundred and fifty seven. Give the IUPAC name of X, and explain why X has the higher boiling point. Pause here to answer.

The carboxyl carbon is carbon one, and the chain has four carbons, with a methyl on carbon three. So X is three-methylbutanoic acid. Two-methylpropanoic acid leaves out the carboxyl carbon. For the boiling point, similar molar masses mean similar dispersion forces, and both hydrogen bond. But X's molecules form dimers, held by two hydrogen bonds, with dipole-dipole forces too. So more energy is needed to separate them.

Last one. Butanoic acid and butan-one-ol are both colourless liquids. Describe a chemical test that would distinguish them, including a balanced equation for any reaction. Then explain why only one of them reacts. Pause here to answer.

Add sodium hydrogen carbonate. Butanoic acid fizzes, giving sodium butanoate, water and carbon dioxide. Butan-one-ol shows no change. Why? Butanoate's charge is shared over two oxygens, so butanoic acid is a stronger acid than carbonic acid, and it gives hydrogen carbonate a proton. The alcohol's charge would sit on one oxygen, so it's far too weak. Saying both react because both have an O H is the trap.
So the carboxyl group explains the high boiling points, and why these acids give up a proton. Next: what happens when a carboxylic acid meets an alcohol, and makes something that smells like fruit.
